Also known as: Pinguicula. Carnivorous plants in the Lentibulariaceae family with sticky leaves that trap insects, include temperate and tropical species.
Cone-bearing evergreen trees and shrubs, include pines, spruces, firs, and cedars, provide year-round structure.
The oldest known living organisms on Earth, with gnarled, wind-sculpted forms found at high elevations in the American West. Some specimens exceed 5,000 years old.
Evergreen conifers in the Pinaceae family with needle-like leaves and woody cones, many species are long-lived and widely planted for timber, shelter, and ornament.
Tropical climbing vine in the Piperaceae family — the world's most traded spice. Produces clusters of small drupes that are dried to make black, white, or green peppercorns.
Deciduous tree in the Anacardiaceae family native to Central Asia, producing green-kerneled nuts that split open when ripe. Thrives in hot, arid climates.
Floating rosettes resembling lettuce. Spreads rapidly. Invasive in warm climates. Provides shade. Check local regulations.
Also known as: Garden pea. Cool-season legume vegetables in the Fabaceae family, prefer cooler temperatures and need support for climbing varieties.
Edible-podded peas in the Fabaceae family, entire pod is eaten, prefer cool weather.
Also known as: Mangetout. Flat-podded peas in the Fabaceae family, entire pod is eaten, popular in Asian cuisine.
Massive deciduous tree with distinctive mottled bark that peels in patches to reveal cream, green, and tan colors. The most widely planted urban street tree worldwide.

Also known as: Swedish begonia, Creeping Charlie (houseplant). Easy trailing houseplant in the Lamiaceae family with glossy, scalloped round leaves and occasional spikes of pale lavender flowers; neither Swedish nor an ivy, it became famous on the White House Oval Office mantel.
Stone-mimicking succulent that resembles a split boulder, closely related to lithops but slightly larger. Native to South Africa.
Epiphytic fern in the Polypodiaceae family that can survive extreme drought by curling up and appearing dead.
Delicate-looking shrub with fine, serrated leaflets; young plants have coppery new growth. Sensitive to changes in light and humidity.
Also known as: Cape leadwort. Sprawling subtropical shrub with clusters of sky-blue phlox-like flowers blooming profusely from spring through fall. Excellent for fences, arbors, and containers.
Also known as: Frangipani. Tropical tree famous for its intensely fragrant, waxy flowers in white, yellow, pink, or red; widely associated with Hawaiian leis.
Also known as: Kusamaki. Conifer-like evergreen with narrow leaves, popular for bonsai and topiary.
Finely textured tropical shrub with lacy, compound leaves; can be pruned into tree form. Sensitive to drafts and dry air.
Emergent aquatic plants in the Pontederiaceae family with spikes of blue flowers, ideal for pond margins.
Floating aquatic with purple flowers. Highly invasive—illegal in some areas. Provides shade and filtration. Check local regulations.
Also known as: Cottonwood. Fast-growing deciduous trees valued for shade, windbreaks, and timber. Lombardy poplar is one of the most recognizable columnar trees.
Deciduous tree famous for leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze. Brilliant golden-yellow fall color. Pando in Utah is the world's largest organism by mass.
Succulent-like leaves with bright flowers in many colors; thrives in hot, dry, poor soil.
Also known as: Spekboom. Small-leaved succulent often confused with jade; drought-tolerant, can be bonsai-trained. Native to South Africa.

Delicate alpine perennials forming rosettes of leaves with clusters of jewel-toned flowers in spring, native to mountain meadows and rocky crevices of Europe and Asia where they endure harsh winters under snow cover.
Deciduous tree in the Rosaceae family producing edible nuts inside fuzzy drupes, closely related to peach. Beautiful pink-white spring blossoms.

Also known as: Chinese plum, Japanese apricot, Mei, Ume. Small deciduous tree in the Rosaceae family that flowers on bare branches in late winter with fragrant white, pink, or red blossoms; celebrated in East Asian art, and its sour fruit is pickled as umeboshi and made into plum wine.
Smooth-skinned peaches in the Rosaceae family, genetic variant of peach, require winter chill.
Ornamental cherry with clouds of pink or white spring blossoms; iconic in Japanese gardens.
Tropical tree in the Myrtaceae family with fragrant pink or white-fleshed fruits, fast-growing and adaptable.
Ferns with divided, often variegated fronds; table fern is common. Non-toxic to pets.
Deciduous fruit trees in the Lythraceae family with jewel-like seeds, drought-tolerant once established.
Also known as: Pyracantha. Thorny evergreen shrub with masses of small white spring flowers followed by spectacular clusters of orange, red, or yellow berries in autumn and winter.
Deciduous fruit trees in the Rosaceae family with sweet, juicy flesh, most varieties need cross-pollination.
Majestic deciduous and evergreen trees in the Fagaceae family, provide shade and wildlife habitat, many species are long-lived.
Spring tuber with layered, rose-like flowers. Soak tubers before planting. Plant in fall (mild) or spring. Dormant after bloom.
Fast-growing root vegetables in the Brassicaceae family, prefer cool weather and can be planted multiple times per season.
Also known as: Mooli, Chinese radish. Large white radishes in the Brassicaceae family, popular in Asian cuisine, fast-growing.
Native prairie wildflower with distinctive drooping yellow or red-brown petals surrounding a tall central cone.
Prairie native with drooping yellow petals around a tall cone; drought tolerant.
Fast-growing climber with fenestrated leaves; resembles small Monstera but is Rhaphidophora. Easy care.
Slow-growing, clumping palm with fan-shaped leaves, very low-maintenance and tolerant of low light.
Perennial vegetable grown for its tart, red or green stalks used in pies, jams, and sauces. Only the stalks are edible — the leaves contain toxic oxalic acid.
Forest cactus that blooms in spring, with rounded leaf segments.
Epiphytic jungle cacti with branching, often pendulous stems; spineless and ideal for hanging baskets.
Tropical coastal trees adapted to saltwater environments with distinctive aerial prop roots. Vital to coastal ecosystems, providing habitat and shoreline protection.
Flowering shrubs in the Ericaceae family, part of the Rhododendron genus, prefer acidic soil and partial shade.
Also known as: Redcurrant, Blackcurrant. Deciduous shrubs in the Grossulariaceae family with red, black, or white berries, used for jams and fresh eating.
Deciduous shrub in the Grossulariaceae family with tart green or red berries, popular for pies and preserves.

Also known as: False acacia, Robinia. Fast-growing deciduous tree in the Fabaceae family with pinnate leaves, paired thorns, and drooping clusters of fragrant white pea flowers in late spring that make prized honey; rot-resistant timber, a nitrogen fixer, and invasive far outside its native range.
Classic flowering shrubs in the Rosaceae family with fragrant blooms, require good air circulation.
Disease-resistant, continuously blooming landscape rose that revolutionized home rose growing. Requires minimal maintenance compared to traditional hybrid tea roses.
Roses with long canes that need support; repeat-blooming or once-blooming depending on cultivar.
Also known as: Blackberry. Perennial cane fruits in the Rosaceae family, produce fruit on second-year canes, can be trailing or erect varieties.
Also known as: Red raspberry. Perennial cane fruits in the Rosaceae family, produce fruit on second-year canes (floricane) or first-year canes (primocane) depending on variety.
Also known as: Gloriosa daisy. Herbaceous perennials in the Asteraceae family with bright yellow daisy-like flowers and dark centers, native wildflowers.
Also known as: Garden sorrel. Perennial herb in the Polygonaceae family with tangy, lemony leaves from oxalic acid. Used in soups, salads, and sauces. French sorrel has milder flavor.
Perennial grass in the Poaceae family. Tropical crop for sugar and ethanol. Tall canes store sucrose. Ratoons (regrowth) for multiple harvests.
Also known as: Duck potato. Aquatic pond plant (Sagittaria)—not the houseplant Arrowhead plant (Syngonium). Arrow-shaped leaves; grows in shallow water or pond edges. Edible tubers (duck potato).
Fast-growing, water-loving trees and shrubs with flexible branches and early-spring catkins, ranging from towering white willows to shrubby pussy and dappled willows.
Iconic deciduous tree with gracefully cascading branches that sweep to the ground. Fast-growing; often planted near water features and ponds for dramatic silhouette.

Also known as: Ornamental sage, Garden salvia. Herbaceous perennials and annuals in the Lamiaceae family grown for long-blooming spikes of purple, blue, red, or pink flowers; many are drought-tolerant and loved by hummingbirds. Culinary sage is listed under Herbs.
Salvia with violet-blue flower spikes; long blooming; drought tolerant once established.
Aromatic evergreen herbs in the Lamiaceae family, drought-tolerant once established, can grow as shrub or groundcover.
Upright perennial with lavender-blue flower spikes and silvery foliage; aromatic.
Deciduous shrubs in the Adoxaceae family with clusters of dark berries, popular for health benefits and jellies.
Carnivorous plants with modified leaves forming pitcher-shaped traps, include temperate and tropical species.
Also known as: Trumpet pitcher. North American pitcher plants native to boggy regions. Upright or hooded pitchers trap insects. Require winter dormancy. Can be grown outdoors in zones 6-9.
Also known as: Rockfoil. Diverse alpine genus with cushion, mat, or rosette forms. Flowers in white, pink, or yellow. Many species for rock gardens.

Also known as: Pincushion flower. Charming perennial with delicate, domed flower heads studded with pin-like stamens in lavender, blue, pink, white, and deep burgundy; a pollinator magnet blooming from early summer to frost.
Native prairie grass with blue-green summer foliage turning orange-red in fall; compact, drought tolerant.
Epiphytic cacti native to tropical forests, require different care from desert cacti with higher humidity needs.
Also known as: Crab cactus. Forest cactus that blooms in late fall, similar to Christmas cactus but with pointed leaf segments.
Also known as: True Christmas cactus. Forest cactus that blooms around Christmas, requires cool temperatures and reduced light to flower, has rounded leaf segments.
Early spring bulb with blue star flowers. Naturalizes well. Plant in fall. Dormant after bloom.
Early spring bulb with blue bell flowers. Siberian squill naturalizes well. Plant in fall. Dormant after bloom.

Also known as: Silver satin pothos, Silver vine. Trailing vine with heart-shaped, matte green leaves covered in silvery spots and patches. Not a true pothos despite the common name; belongs to the genus Scindapsus.
Annual grass in the Poaceae family. Cereal for bread, whiskey, and feed. Winter rye is cold-hardy cover crop. Tolerates poor soil.
Also known as: Mirliton. Tender squash (mirliton) with edible fruit, shoots, and roots; vigorous vine.
Low, mat-forming succulents with small leaves; yellow or pink flowers, drought-tolerant.
Also known as: White-fleshed dragon fruit. Cactus fruits in the Cactaceae family, also known as pitaya, popular tropical fruit with striking appearance.

Also known as: Hen and chicks. Hardy succulents in the Crassulaceae family known as hen and chicks, form rosettes and produce offsets. Extremely cold hardy and drought tolerant. Excellent for rock gardens, alpine gardens, and containers.
The tallest trees on Earth, native to the foggy coastal forests of California and Oregon, with soft reddish bark and flat needles.
Also known as: Wellingtonia. The largest trees on Earth by volume, native to the western Sierra Nevada with massive trunks and spongy, fire-resistant bark.
Annual in the Pedaliaceae family. Seeds for oil and tahini. Drought and heat tolerant. Capsules shatter when ripe—harvest carefully.
Non-vascular bryophytes that require constant moisture and high humidity, absorb water through leaves.
Tall prairie native with large yellow flowers; leaves orient north-south; drought tolerant.
Tall prairie native with large heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers; deep taproot.
Also known as: Plum tomato. Plum tomato in the Solanaceae family with meaty, low-moisture flesh, ideal for sauces, paste, and canning.
Small, sweet tomatoes in the Solanaceae family, prolific and easy to grow, ideal for salads and snacking.
Also known as: Aubergine. Warm-season fruiting vegetable in the Solanaceae family, also known as aubergine, requires long growing season.
Slender, elongated eggplant varieties popular in Asian cuisine. Includes Japanese, Chinese, and other types with thin skin, few seeds, and tender flesh that cooks quickly.
Underground tuber vegetables in the Solanaceae family, require hilling (mounding soil) around stems as they grow.
Native perennial with yellow flower plumes in fall; important for pollinators; drought tolerant.
Tall native prairie grass with golden fall color and feathery bronze seed heads; warm-season grass.
Annual grass in the Poaceae family. Grain, syrup, forage, and biofuel. Drought tolerant. Grain, sweet, and broomcorn types.
Variegated peace lily with white speckling on green leaves; smaller than Sensation, good for tabletops.
Also known as: Sensation peace lily. Large cultivar of peace lily with broad, glossy leaves; can reach 4–6 feet. Low-light tolerant and shows need for water by drooping.
Aroids with white spathes and dark green foliage, excellent air purifiers, droop dramatically when thirsty as a watering indicator. Includes various cultivars ranging from compact to large.
Cool-season leafy green in the Amaranthaceae family, bolts quickly in heat, best grown in spring and fall.
Versatile shrub with spring or summer flowers; mound-forming or cascading forms.
Fine-textured native prairie grass with fragrant fall blooms; forms neat mounds, excellent for borders.
Fuzzy, silver-gray foliage that feels like lamb's wool; purple flower spikes in summer.
Also known as: Giant bird of paradise. Large tropical plant with banana-like leaves and striking white and blue crane-shaped flowers. Grows to 6m outdoors; popular as dramatic indoor foliage plant.

Compact flowering plants in the Gesneriaceae family with fuzzy leaves and colorful blooms, avoid getting water on leaves. Includes various cultivars with different flower colors, single, double, or ruffled flowers.
Prayer plants in the Marantaceae family with colorful, patterned leaves that fold up at night.
Fall-blooming perennial flowering plants in the Asteraceae family, provide late-season color with daisy-like flowers.
Native aster with blue-purple flowers in fall; smooth leaves; drought tolerant.
Native fall bloomer with purple daisy flowers; attracts butterflies; prefers moist soil.
Perennial herb in the Boraginaceae family with large hairy leaves. Traditionally used externally for bruises and sprains. Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids—do not ingest; mild toxicity to pets.
Variegated arrowhead with white and green leaves; trailing or compact depending on pruning. Easy-care aroid.
Also known as: Pink Splash. Pink-toned arrowhead plants with leaves ranging from soft pink to vibrant magenta, including solid and splash-patterned varieties.
Arrowhead plant with cream and green variegation; vining or compact depending on pruning. Easy-care aroid.
Deciduous shrubs in the Oleaceae family with fragrant spring flowers in shades of purple, pink, white, and blue.
Tropical evergreen tree in the Myrtaceae family whose aromatic, unopened flower buds are dried to produce cloves — one of the world's oldest known spices.
Hardy annual flowering plants in the Asteraceae family with bright yellow, orange, or red flowers, excellent for pest control.
Large, bold flowers in yellow or orange; pest-repellent and excellent for cutting.
Also known as: Tamarindo, Indian Date. Long-lived tropical tree producing pod-like fruits with tangy pulp widely used in cuisines and beverages worldwide.
Also known as: Pyrethrum. Colorful daisy-like flowers in pink, red, or white with ferny foliage; natural source of pyrethrin insecticide.
Edible greens from the common dandelion; slightly bitter, nutritious, best when young. Roots and flowers also edible.
Also known as: Bogor Moss, Mini Moss, Christmas Moss (similar). Fast-growing aquatic moss that clings to surfaces, ideal for aquascaping and providing fry shelter.
Deciduous conifer with feathery foliage and distinctive "knees"; tolerates wet or swampy sites.
Also known as: Split-leaf philodendron. Large, deeply lobed Philodendron; can grow into a small tree. Now classified as Thaumatophyllum bipinnatifidum.
Deeply lobed, compact Philodendron; self-heading, does not climb. Dense foliage habit.
The tropical tree whose seeds are fermented and processed to produce chocolate, cocoa butter, and cocoa powder—one of the world's most economically important crops.
Also known as: Eastern White Cedar, Northern White Cedar. Dense, evergreen conifer widely used for hedges, privacy screens, and windbreaks.

Also known as: Clock vine, Thunbergia. Fast twining vine in the Acanthaceae family with heart-shaped leaves and cheerful orange, yellow, or white flowers with dark purple-black throats from summer to frost; grown as an annual on trellises and in hanging baskets.
Also known as: Mother of thyme. Low mat-forming herb with tiny flowers; aromatic, walkable groundcover.
Also known as: Basswood, Tilia. Deciduous shade tree with heart-shaped leaves and intensely fragrant cream-colored flowers in summer. Major urban and park tree throughout Europe.
Epiphytic plants in the Bromeliaceae family that grow without soil, absorb water and nutrients through their leaves.
Also known as: Graybeard. Air plant (Tillandsia usneoides) that hangs in draping strands. No roots in soil - absorbs moisture through leaves. Grows on trees in Southeast US.
Large, sculptural air plant with silvery curly leaves. Xeromorphic - needs less water than most Tillandsia. Drought tolerant.
Trailing plant with thick, striped leaves in pink, green, and cream; compact, upright-then-cascading habit.
Trailing plant with vivid purple foliage and small pink flowers; can be grown indoors or outdoors.
Also known as: Spiderwort. Fast-growing trailing plants in the Commelinaceae family with colorful striped or solid leaves.
Also known as: Oyster plant. Root vegetable in the Asteraceae family with long white roots and oyster-like flavor.
Also known as: Meadow clover. Perennial legume in the Fabaceae family. Forage and cover crop. Nitrogen-fixing; pink flowers. Short-lived perennial (2–3 years).
Low-growing perennial legume commonly used as a ground cover, living mulch, and forage crop. Fixes nitrogen in the soil. Attractive to pollinators with white flower heads.
Mild, delicate sprouts similar to alfalfa. Harvest in 5–7 days. Rinse 2–3× daily.
Aromatic, slightly bitter sprouts. Curry-like. Harvest in 4–6 days. Rinse 2× daily.
Annual grass in the Poaceae family. World's major cereal crop. Bread wheat (T. aestivum) and durum. Spring and winter types by planting season.
Spring-blooming bulbous perennials in the Liliaceae family, planted in fall for spring flowers, many varieties available.
Emergent wetland plants in the Typhaceae family, grow in shallow water or wet soil, can be invasive.
Also known as: American Elm, White Elm, Water Elm. Iconic deciduous shade tree with a vase-shaped canopy, once the dominant street tree in North America.
Graceful deciduous or semi-evergreen tree with small leaves, fine branching, and attractive mottled bark that flakes to reveal orange, grey, and cream. The most popular species for bonsai.
Acidic soil-loving berry shrubs in the Ericaceae family, require pH 4.5-5.5 and often need cross-pollination.
Low-growing evergreen shrubs in the Ericaceae family, require acidic soil and constant moisture, popular for Thanksgiving.
Large genus of trees and shrubs found across Africa, Australia, and the Americas. Iconic savanna trees with umbrella-shaped canopies. Australian wattles are the national floral emblem.
Monopodial orchids with strap leaves and large, colorful flowers. Often grown bare-root in baskets or with minimal media. Need high light and humidity.

Climbing orchid (Vanilla planifolia) that produces the vanilla bean. Grows as a vine; needs support. Tropical, high humidity and warmth. Also grown commercially as one of the world's most valuable spices.
Symbiotic organism (fungus + algae/cyanobacteria) growing on bark, rocks, or soil. Rarely cultivated; use for identification or terrarium accent.
Tall biennial with velvety leaves and yellow flower spike; drought tolerant; self-seeds.
Clusters of small flowers in purple, pink, or white on wiry stems; heat-tolerant perennial that attracts butterflies.
Clusters of small flowers in purple, pink, red, or white; heat-tolerant, butterfly-friendly.
Native perennial with purple flowers; thrives in moist soils; attracts butterflies.
Also known as: Veronica. Cottage garden perennial with upright spikes of small blue, purple, pink, or white flowers. Excellent for pollinators and long-lasting in the border.
Native perennial with white candelabra flower spikes; attracts butterflies; prefers moist soil.
Deciduous and evergreen shrubs in the Adoxaceae family with showy flowers, colorful berries, and fall foliage.
Annual legume in the Fabaceae family. Broad bean; cool-season crop. Large seeds for drying or fresh use. Some avoid raw—contains vicine.

Also known as: Amazon water lily, Victoria water lily. The largest water lily in the world, with circular floating pads up to 3m in diameter that can support the weight of a child. White flowers bloom at night.
Also known as: Azuki bean, Red bean. Small red beans in the Fabaceae family, very popular in Chinese and Japanese cuisine, used in desserts.
Fast-growing legumes in the Fabaceae family, very popular in Chinese cuisine, can be sprouted.
Annual legume in the Fabaceae family. Drought and heat tolerant. Black-eyed pea, crowder types. Grown for dried peas and forage.
Also known as: Yard-long bean. Long Asian bean in the Fabaceae family, can reach 3 feet, similar to green beans but more heat-tolerant.
Evergreen groundcover in the Apocynaceae family with glossy leaves and spring flowers, can be invasive.
Also known as: Johnny-jump-up. Small pansy-like flowers with distinctive markings; Johnny-jump-up and violas are cold-tolerant.
Cold-tolerant flowers with face-like markings in many colors; plant in fall or early spring.
Also known as: Wine grape. Perennial climbing vines in the Vitaceae family, produce clusters of berries, require pruning and support structures.
Architectural shrub with trumpet flowers in spring; green, gold, or variegated foliage.

One of the most unusual plants on Earth — a living fossil from the Namib Desert. Each plant produces only two leaves in its entire lifetime, which grow continuously and split into straps. Can live over 1,000 years.
Vigorous, long-lived climbing vine famous for its cascading clusters of fragrant purple, blue, pink, or white flowers in spring. Iconic in Japanese gardens, particularly the famous wisteria tunnels.
Vigorous climbing vines in the Fabaceae family with cascading clusters of fragrant flowers, require strong support.
Also known as: Indian Ginseng, Winter Cherry, Poison Gooseberry. Adaptogenic herb from India with velvety leaves and small orange-red berries enclosed in papery husks.
Living fossil discovered in 1994 in a remote canyon in Australia. Thought to have been extinct for 2 million years. Distinctive bubbly, chocolate-brown bark.
Tropical aroids with large arrow-shaped leaves (elephant ears), require high humidity and consistent moisture.

Also known as: Everlasting, Paper daisy, Golden everlasting. Australian daisy in the Asteraceae family whose papery, straw-textured bracts in gold, orange, red, pink, and white keep their color for years when dried; the classic everlasting for wreaths and dried bouquets.
Iconic tree-like yucca of the Mojave Desert with twisted branches and spiky leaf clusters, a symbol of the American Southwest.
Also known as: Giant yucca. Drought-tolerant plants in the Asparagaceae family with sword-like leaves, can grow into small trees.
Also known as: Zanzibar gem, Eternity plant. Extremely low-maintenance plant in the Araceae family with glossy leaves and rhizomes that store water, virtually indestructible.
Also known as: Raven ZZ plant, Black ZZ. Dark purple-black variety of ZZ plant, same easy-care as standard ZZ, new growth emerges green and darkens with age.
Also known as: Dwarf ZZ plant. Compact cultivar of Zamioculcas zamiifolia with shorter, more tightly clustered dark green leaflets on chunky stems.
Also known as: Compact calla. Compact Zantedeschia with smaller spathes. Colors include pink, yellow, orange. Toxic to pets.
Also known as: Arum lily. Tuberous aroid with elegant spathe flowers in white, pink, or dark cultivars. Grown as houseplant or garden bulb; goes dormant after bloom.
Also known as: Maize. Tall grain crop in the Poaceae family, requires pollination from wind or manual assistance, plant in blocks for better pollination.
Rhizomatous herbs in the Zingiberaceae family, essential spice in Chinese cuisine, can be grown from store-bought rhizomes.
Also known as: Youth-and-old-age. Annual flowers in the Asteraceae family with bright, daisy-like blooms in many colors, easy to grow from seed.
Also known as: Chinese date, Red date. Deciduous fruit trees in the Rhamnaceae family, also known as Chinese date or red date, drought-tolerant.
Intergeneric hybrid between Graptopetalum and Echeveria, forming compact rosettes with thick, fleshy leaves in pastel hues that intensify with sun stress.
